 ‘Madden’ Review: Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale Go for Broke in a Cartoonish Biopic From David O. Russell That’s Strictly for Football Fanatics
 Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller and John Mulaney also star in the Prime Video original, which traces John Madden's career as coach and commentator alongside his buddy Al Davis.

 Imagine being cornered at a party while sober by a wired cokehead determined to tell you a long, painstakingly detailed story without pausing for breath and you might have some idea of the exhausting experience of watching Madden . Full disclosure: I have almost no knowledge of or interest in football beyond religious devotion to all five seasons of Friday Night Lights . Which should in theory disqualify me from reviewing David O. Russell ’s feverish chronicle of John Madden’s career as legendary head coach for the Oakland Raiders and longtime NFL telecast commentator. But hey, the job’s the job.

 Even if I were passionate about pigskin, however, I can’t imagine getting much pleasure from this cartoonish biodrama, led by the kind of stunt acting from both principals that never lets you forget they are Giving a Performance. (Think Tom Cruise in Tropic Thunder . Or Digger .) This means that despite hurling themselves into their roles with gusto, there’s little to no risk of forming a human emotional connection with Nicolas Cage ’s Madden or Christian Bale ’s Al Davis, the longtime friend who was the Raiders’ owner and general manager.
 Madden 
 The Bottom Line 
 Should come with a concussion warning.
 Release date : Weds., Nov. 18
 Cast : Nicolas Cage, Christian Bale, Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller, John Mulaney, Shane Gillis, Simms May, Luke Klein, Joel Murray, Mark Medrano
 Director : David O. Russell
 Screenwriter : David O. Russell, Cambron Clark
 Rated R,
 1 hour 50 minutes 
 Cage is encased in a fat suit so bulky he looks like a line drawing out of Family Guy , while Bale goes for a receding hairline, a mouth locked in a Harvey Keitel grimace and a chewy Brooklyn accent, matched by that of Sienna Miller as Davis’ wife Carol. Meanwhile, both Miller and Kathryn Hahn as Madden’s wife Virginia appear to have gone wig-shopping with Nicole Kidman. That’s a let-down coming from the director of one of the 21st century’s great hair movies, American Hustle .
 Co-written by Russell with Cambron Clark, Madden kicks off in 1976 when the Pro Football Hall of Famer’s days on the field are far behind him and he has racked up an impressive streak of winning seasons for the Raiders. But Super Bowl triumph remains elusive. That changes the following year when the team defeats the Minnesota Vikings to claim victory in Super Bowl IX.
 Virginia has bought John’s vague promises that he would take a breather once that milestone had been reached, finally spending more time with his wife and their sons Mike (Simms May) and Joe (Luke Klein) and maybe renewing their wedding vows. (He’s so consumed by his work that he can’t even remember the boys’ ages.) Having earned a pilot’s license, Virginia also hopes to coax John past his fear of flying and take him for a spin. But as Al keeps reminding him, football is who he is, so John stays on for another two seasons before a bleeding ulcer forces him into retirement.
 Connoisseurs of gonzo Cage performances might get a kick out of his characterization. The actor makes Madden a football visionary, with thousands of strategic plays in his head — or scrawled across the screen in noughts-and-crosses graphics. He’s a sports genius who can sometimes come across as borderline simple-minded, which adds to the innate sweetness Cage brings to the role. Even if he’s an absentee husband and dad much of the time, John’s love for his wife and sons is never in doubt. It’s just that they are in constant competition with his love for the game and his team.
 Even so, the conflict always feels low-stakes, even when the unaccustomed inactivity of retirement has John acting crazy, muttering football philosophy to the family’s dog. Unable to separate himself entirely from the game, he accepts an offer from CBS Sports to provide football commentary, his discursive, stream-of-consciousness patter ignoring the mandate to follow the lead of sportscaster Pat Summerall (Joel Murray), much to the latter’s frustration.
 But Russell skips right over any friction in their adjustment period, jumping ahead to the on-air bonhomie that made Madden and Summerall one of the most celebrated football commentary duos in sports broadcasting history. There’s an almost manic level of excitement from John as he scrawls complex plays onto a telestrator (like a not-hot version of Steve Kornacki on election nights), while Pat seems completely comfortable playing the amused straight man.
 The other significant thread starts with overtures from Trip Hawkins ( John Mulaney ), founder of video game company Electronic Arts, who masterminds what would go on to become a major success story with Madden NFL . John is skeptical at first, unimpressed with the clunky pixel figures Trip and his team of nerds demonstrate in an initial presentation of the sports game. But once John hands over the fat ring-binder file where he has recorded every play, the techies perfect the product, making it one of the top sellers in video game history.
 Al strenuously objects to John sharing his playbook, insisting that the contents are a vital part of his legacy with the Raiders that will ensure his place in “The Afterlife Football Hall of Fame.” But that recurring motif is about as substantial as the mockumentary setup that has Virginia addressing the camera from an armchair early on. 
 Both wives are shortchanged by the script. Moments of drama like Virginia’s divorce threats or Carol’s stroke and subsequent period in a coma fizzle before they can gain much steam. Shane Gillis , the stand-up more famous for his racist, misogynistic and homophobic slurs than his comedy, appears as Madden’s idolizing next-door neighbor but brings very little to the table.
 The heart of the film, ostensibly, is the friendship between John and Al, but it’s hard to invest when the characters never feel much like real people. For anyone without an insatiable appetite for American football history, the story is seldom of much interest, which perhaps explains why three credited editors have cut the film at such a rollicking pace, and why Russell stuffs in period needle drops at every opportunity.
 Madden is an improvement on his last feature, the laborious 2022 screwball comedy Amsterdam . But like that movie it’s busy and abrasive, without being entertaining beyond the curiosity of Nicolas Cage bouncing around in a mound of prosthetics.
